title: Hope and fear march together
hookLine: Hecaton: stop hoping and you'll stop fearing, for they're chained together

cards: You apply for the apartment, and for a week you're floating. You've already placed the couch. You've picked the coffee shop on the corner.
Then, around day four, the floating turns. What if they say no? What if someone else got there first?

You check your email every ten minutes. The hope and the dread arrived together, holding hands. Seneca has a line for this, in the second half of his fifth letter, and he borrowed it from another Stoic.

teach.b: He found it, Seneca says, in Hecaton, whom he calls our Hecaton: one of the Stoics' own. Hecaton says: stop hoping, and you'll stop fearing. It sounds bleak at first.
Seneca explains with a picture: one chain fastens the prisoner and the soldier guarding him. Wherever one went, the other went too. Hope and fear are like that, as different as they look.
Both belong to a mind hanging in suspense, worried about what's coming. Why? Because, Seneca says, we don't fit ourselves to the present.
We send our thoughts far ahead. Foresight, one of the great gifts of being human, turns against us. Animals run from a danger they can see, and once they've escaped, they're at peace.
We're tormented by what's coming and by what's already past. No one, he says, is miserable only because of the present. Seneca isn't saying give up on everything, or don't plan, or stop caring.
This letter isn't an argument against hope as any faith teaches it.

teach.h: NOT ALL HOPE: THE ANXIOUS KIND.
teach.b: The target is narrower: the anxious, future-gripping kind of hoping, the kind that's really fear in a nicer coat.
Bring the mind back to today, and both lose their grip at once. The chain goes slack.

how: Stoic practice includes noticing when the mind has run ahead into the future, and bringing it back to the present task, where neither anxious hope nor fear has much hold.

games.q: you're a Roman prisoner, chained to a soldier. you want to cross the room. what happens?
o: the guard comes too, wherever you go.
games.why: that's Seneca's picture: hope and fear look different, but where one goes, the other follows.

practice: Bring to mind something you're hoping for right now, a result, a reply, a yes, and look just behind the hope: is a fear walking alongside, what if it doesn't happen? Don't push either away; just see them side by side on one chain.
Then come back to this moment, your breath, your hands, the room, where neither one has arrived yet.

wordCard.voice: Hecaton. The Stoic Seneca quotes: stop hoping, and you'll stop fearing, since anxious hope and fear are chained like a prisoner and his guard.

orig.note: Latin: you will cease to fear if you cease to hope, Hecaton's line as Seneca gives it.

carryVoice: Your line: chained together. Here, in this moment, neither the hope nor the fear has arrived. Until tomorrow.
